subject: math
title: Data and Graphs: Histograms, Broken-Line Graphs, Mean, Median, Mode and Misleading Graphs
seo_title: Grade 6 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Mean, Median, Mode, Histograms (Free, Answer Key)
standard_text: Determine the range and the measures of central tendency for data sets, and use these measures to compare data sets; analyse different sets of data presented in various ways, including in misleading graphs, by asking and answering questions about the data and drawing conclusions
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on data and graphs for the Ontario curriculum: discrete and continuous data, histograms, broken-line graphs, mean, median, mode and range, comparing data sets and spotting misleading graphs. 100 questions with an answer key, good EQAO practice.
key_big: Mean, median, mode and range describe a data set; check the scale before you trust a graph.
key_sub: Mean = total ÷ number of values. Median = the middle value in order. Mode = the most common value. Range = highest − lowest. Discrete data is counted; continuous data is measured.
body_html:
Discrete and continuous data

Discrete data is counted, so it has only certain values, such as 0, 1, 2, 3 goals. Continuous data is measured, so it can be any value in a range, such as 148.6 cm or 41.35 s.

Kind of dataHow you get itExamplesGood graph
DiscreteCountPets, goals, students on a busBar graph, line plot
ContinuousMeasureHeight, mass, time, temperatureHistogram, broken-line graph

Histograms and broken-line graphs

A histogram groups continuous data into equal intervals. The bars touch, because one interval ends where the next one begins.

Example 1

How many students spent 40 minutes or more on homework?

40 minutes or more means the bars from 40 to 50 and from 50 to 60: 9 + 4 = 13.

Answer: 13 students

A broken-line graph shows how continuous data changes over time. The points are joined by straight lines. A steep line means a fast change.

Example 2

By how many degrees did the temperature rise from Tuesday to Thursday?

Tuesday −8 °C, Thursday 2 °C. From −8 up to 0 is 8 degrees, and from 0 up to 2 is 2 more: 8 + 2 = 10.

Answer: 10 °C

Mean, median, mode and range

MeasureHow to find itFor 6, 3, 8, 3, 5
MeanAdd the values, then divide by how many there are25 ÷ 5 = 5
MedianPut the values in order and take the middle one3, 3, 5, 6, 8 → 5
ModeThe value that appears most often3
RangeHighest − lowest8 − 3 = 5

With an even number of values, the median is halfway between the two middle values. One very large or very small value (an outlier) pulls the mean toward it, so the median often describes a typical value better.

To compare two data sets, compare their means or medians (which is higher?) and their ranges (which is more spread out?). A smaller range means the data is more consistent.

Misleading graphs

Before you believe a graph or a claim, check: Does the scale start at 0? Are the spaces on the scale equal? How many people were asked, and who?

Example 3

A sign says, “Everyone loves the new playground: 100% of the kids we asked said yes!” They asked 3 kids. Is the claim supported?

3 kids is far too small a sample to speak for everyone.

Answer: No

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Giving the highest value as the modeThe mode is the value that appears most often
Finding the median without putting the values in orderOrder the values first, then take the middle
Dividing by the wrong number for the meanDivide by how many values there are, including any zeros
Giving the biggest number as the rangeRange = highest − lowest
Judging bars by height when the scale does not start at 0Read the real values and subtract
Trusting a survey of a few people, or of people chosen in one placeAsk how many and who was asked

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about data in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: In Grade 6, students tell discrete from continuous data, read and make histograms and broken-line graphs, find the mean, median, mode and range, compare data sets, and spot misleading graphs. Data questions also appear on the Grade 6 EQAO math assessment.

faq.q: What is the difference between discrete and continuous data?
faq.a: Discrete data is counted and has only certain values, such as the number of pets. Continuous data is measured and can be any value in a range, such as height, mass, time or temperature.

faq.q: What is the difference between a histogram and a bar graph?
faq.a: A histogram shows continuous data grouped into equal intervals, so its bars touch. A bar graph shows categories or discrete data, so its bars have gaps between them.

faq.q: How can a graph be misleading?
faq.a: A scale that does not start at 0 makes small differences look big, and unequal spaces on a scale distort the data. Conclusions can also mislead when the sample is very small or the people asked were not chosen fairly.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of pets each student has
items.e: Pets are counted: 0, 1, 2, 3 … Nobody has 2.5 pets, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The height of each student in centimetres
items.e: Height is measured. It can be any value in a range, such as 148.6 cm, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The time each student takes to skate one lap of the rink
items.e: Time is measured. It can be 41 s, 41.3 s or 41.35 s, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of goals scored in each hockey game
items.e: Goals are counted. A team can score 3 or 4 goals but not 3.5, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The mass of each pumpkin at a Thanksgiving market
items.e: Mass is measured, so it can be any value, such as 4.25 kg. The data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of people in each canoe on a canoe trip
items.e: People are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The amount of sap collected from each maple tree, in litres
items.e: The amount of sap is measured. It can be 2.4 L or 2.45 L, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of snow days each winter
items.e: Snow days are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The temperature at noon each day in January
items.e: Temperature is measured with a thermometer. It can be −7.5 °C, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of loons counted on the lake each morning
items.e: Loons are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The distance each student runs in the Terry Fox Run, in kilometres
items.e: Distance is measured. A student could run 3.2 km or 3.25 km, so the data is continuous.

items.q:
Is this data discrete or continuous?
The number of books each student read over the summer holidays
items.e: Books are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.

items.q: Which of these is continuous data?
items.e: Sleep is measured in time, so it can be 8.5 or 8.75 hours. The others are counted, so they are discrete.

items.q: Which of these is discrete data?
items.e: Cars are counted in whole numbers. Mass, length and time are measured, so they are continuous.

items.q: What kind of data is each student’s favourite hockey team?
items.e: The answers are team names, not numbers, so the data is qualitative (categories). Discrete and continuous are kinds of number data.

items.q: What kind of data is the number on each player’s hockey jersey?
items.e: Jersey numbers only name the players. Adding them or finding their mean makes no sense, so they are labels: qualitative data, even though they look like numbers.

items.q: Students’ heights are grouped into intervals: 130 to 140 cm, 140 to 150 cm, and so on. Which graph fits best?
items.e: Height is continuous data. A histogram shows continuous data in equal intervals, with bars that touch.

items.q: Why do the bars of a histogram touch?
items.e: In a histogram, one interval ends where the next begins (140 cm is the end of one and the start of the next). There are no gaps in continuous data, so there are no gaps between the bars.

items.q: Which data is best shown on a broken-line graph?
items.e: A broken-line graph shows how continuous data changes over time. The puppy’s mass changes from week to week. The other data is categories, so a bar graph fits better.

items.q: Maya records how many laps each student skates and how long each lap takes. Which is true?
items.e: Laps are counted in whole numbers (discrete). Time is measured and can be any value (continuous).

items.q: How many students took from 6 to 7 minutes?
items.e: Find the bar between 6 and 7 on the time axis. It reaches 9. (7 is the next bar, from 7 to 8 minutes, 6 is the bar before, and 10 is the labelled line above the bar.)

items.q: Which interval has the most students?
items.e: The tallest bar is between 6 and 7 minutes (9 students). The interval with the most data is not the one with the biggest times.

items.q: How many students ran 1 km in less than 6 minutes?
items.e: Less than 6 minutes means the bars from 4 to 5 and from 5 to 6: 2 + 6 = 8. (17 also adds the 6 to 7 bar.)

items.q: How many students ran altogether?
items.e: Add all the bars: 2 + 6 + 9 + 7 + 4 + 2 = 30. (9 is only the tallest bar, and 6 is the number of bars.)

items.q: How many students took 8 minutes or more?
items.e: 8 minutes or more means the bars from 8 to 9 and from 9 to 10: 4 + 2 = 6. (13 also adds the 7 to 8 bar.)

items.q: What was the fastest time?
items.e: The first bar shows that 2 students took from 4 to 5 minutes. A histogram groups the data, so it does not show each exact time.

items.q: How many students are at least 150 cm tall?
items.e: At least 150 cm means the bars from 150 to 160 and from 160 to 170: 12 + 5 = 17. (27 also adds the 140 to 150 bar.)

items.q: How many students are shorter than 150 cm?
items.e: Shorter than 150 cm means the bars from 130 to 140 and from 140 to 150: 3 + 10 = 13. (10 is only one bar.)

items.q: Which interval has the median height?
items.e: There are 30 students, so the median is between the 15th and 16th heights in order. The first two bars hold 3 + 10 = 13 students, so the 14th to 25th students are in the 150 to 160 bar.

items.q: What fraction of the students are 160 cm or taller?
items.e: 5 of the 30 students are in the 160 to 170 bar. 5 out of 30 = 1 out of 6. (1/5 comes from 5 out of 25, 2/5 reads the 150 to 160 bar (12 out of 30), and 1/4 counts the bars, not the students.)

items.q: What was the temperature at noon?
items.e: Go up from “noon” to the point, then across to the scale. The point is on the line for −10, below 0, so it is −10 °C. (10 °C forgets the minus sign.)

items.q: At what time was it warmest?
items.e: The warmest temperature is the highest point on the graph: −6 °C at 2 p.m. (At 8 a.m. it was −18 °C. 18 is the biggest number, but −18 °C is the coldest.)

items.q: By how many degrees did the temperature rise from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m.?
items.e: From −18 °C up to −6 °C: count up the scale. −18 to −6 is 12 degrees. (24 adds 18 and 6, as if one were above 0.)

items.q: Between which two times did the temperature drop the most?
items.e: Look for the steepest line going down. From 4 p.m. to 6 p.m. it fell from −8 °C to −12 °C (4 degrees). From 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. it fell only 2 degrees. In the morning it was rising.

items.q: Use the line to estimate the temperature at 9 a.m.
items.e: 9 a.m. is halfway between 8 a.m. (−18 °C) and 10 a.m. (−14 °C). The line there is at about −16 °C.

items.q: Why are the points on this graph joined with lines?
c: To make the graph look neat
The temperature changes all the time
items.e: Temperature is continuous: it has a value at every moment, not only at the times measured. The lines show how it changed between the points.

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 4?
items.e: Go up from week 4 to the point, then across: it is on the line for 40 cm.

items.q: How much did the sunflower grow from week 3 to week 4?
items.e: Week 3: 25 cm. Week 4: 40 cm. Growth = 40 − 25 = 15 cm. (40 is the height, not the growth.)

items.q: In which week did the sunflower grow the most?
items.e: The steepest part of the line shows the most growth. Week 5 to week 6: 75 − 55 = 20 cm. Every other week it grew 15 cm or less.

items.q: How much did the sunflower grow from week 1 to week 6?
items.e: Week 6: 75 cm. Week 1: 10 cm. 75 − 10 = 65 cm. (75 cm is its height, which includes the 10 cm it already had.)

items.q:
Goals scored by the school hockey team in 8 games:
3, 5, 2, 5, 7, 1, 5, 4
What is the mode?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often. 5 appears 3 times, so the mode is 5 goals. (7 is the highest value, 3 is how many times 5 appears, and 4.5 is the median.)

items.q:
Minutes 5 students spent reading:
12, 7, 15, 9, 20
What is the median?
items.e: In order: 7, 9, 12, 15, 20. The middle value is 12. (15 is the middle of the list before it was put in order, 13 is the range, and 12.6 is the mean.)

items.q:
Laps skated by 6 students:
4, 9, 6, 3, 8, 10
What is the median?
items.e: In order: 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10. With 6 values there are two middle values, 6 and 8. The median is halfway between them: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7. (4.5 uses 6 and 3 from the unordered list, and 14 forgets to divide by 2.)

items.q:
Cans collected by 5 students for the food drive:
12, 15, 9, 14, 10
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 12 + 15 + 9 + 14 + 10 = 60. There are 5 values, so 60 ÷ 5 = 12. (60 is the total, 10 divides by 6, and 6 is the range.)

items.q:
Rain that fell on 4 days in Vancouver (mm):
3.5, 4.2, 2.8, 5.1
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 3.5 + 4.2 + 2.8 + 5.1 = 15.6. Divide by 4: 15.6 ÷ 4 = 3.9 mm. (3.12 divides by 5, and 2.3 is the range.)

items.q:
Temperatures at 7 a.m. in Ottawa for 6 days in March (°C):
−3, 4, −7, 2, 0, 5
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 5 °C, lowest −7 °C. From −7 up to 0 is 7 degrees, and from 0 up to 5 is 5 more: 7 + 5 = 12 °C. (2 ignores the minus sign: 7 − 5. 8 uses −3 instead of the lowest value, −7.)

items.q:
Ages of the swimmers in a lesson:
11, 14, 11, 16, 13, 11, 14
What is the mode?
items.e: 11 appears 3 times, more than any other age, so the mode is 11 years. (16 is the highest age, and 3 is how many times 11 appears.)

items.q:
Points scored by a basketball player in 7 games:
2, 4, 4, 6, 7, 7, 9
What is the mode?
items.e: 4 appears twice and 7 appears twice. Every other value appears once. So there are two modes: 4 and 7.

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 10:
8, 3, 6, 10, 5
What is the mode?
items.e: Each score appears only once, so no value appears most often. There is no mode. (10 is the highest score, and 5 is how many scores there are.)

items.q: Each X is one student. What is the median number of pets?
items.e: There are 17 X’s, so the median is the 9th value in order. Count from the left: 3 students have 0 pets, and the next 6 have 1 pet. The 9th value is 1. (2 is the middle of the number line, not of the data.)
The tallest stack is above 1, so the mode is 1 pet. (6 is the height of that stack, and 4 is the highest value.)

items.q: The mean of Arjun’s 4 math tests is 80. Three of his scores are 75, 82 and 78. What is the 4th score?
items.e: A mean of 80 for 4 tests means the total is 4 × 80 = 320. The first three add to 75 + 82 + 78 = 235. 320 − 235 = 85. (80 is the mean, not the missing score, and 5 uses 3 × 80 instead of 4 × 80.)

items.q: One very large value is added to a data set. Which measure changes the most?
items.e: The mean uses every value, so one very large value pulls it up a lot. The median only moves by one place, and the mode usually does not change.

items.q:
Minutes 5 students took to get to school:
12, 14, 13, 15, 46
Which value best describes a typical time?
items.e: 46 is far from the other values (it is an outlier). It pulls the mean up to 20, which is more than 4 of the 5 times. The median, 14, is in the middle of the usual times.

items.q:
Leah spent this on lunch at school each day for a week:
$4.50, $5.25, $3.75, $6.10, $5.40
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 4.50 + 5.25 + 3.75 + 6.10 + 5.40 = 25.00. Divide by 5 days: $25.00 ÷ 5 = $5.00. ($6.25 divides by 4, and $5.25 is the median, not the mean.)

items.q:
Masses of 6 pumpkins (kg):
3.2, 4.8, 5.5, 2.9, 6.1, 4.5
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 3.2 + 4.8 + 5.5 + 2.9 + 6.1 + 4.5 = 27. There are 6 pumpkins: 27 ÷ 6 = 4.5 kg. (27 is the total, 5.4 divides by 5, and 3.2 is the range.)

items.q:
Times for 5 swimmers in a race (seconds):
10.8, 9.95, 11.2, 10.25, 9.7
What is the median?
items.e: In order: 9.7, 9.95, 10.25, 10.8, 11.2. The middle value is 10.25 s. (11.2 is the middle of the unordered list, 10.38 is the mean, and 1.5 is the range.)

items.q:
Centimetres of snow that fell each day for 6 days:
0, 5, 0, 9, 6, 4
What is the mean?
items.e: Add: 0 + 5 + 0 + 9 + 6 + 4 = 24. There are 6 days, including the 2 days with 0 cm: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm. (6 leaves out the zeros and divides by 4.)

items.q:
Hours of screen time for 5 students on a Saturday:
2, 3, 3, 4, 13
Which statement is true?
c: The mean is greater than the median
items.e: Mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5. Median = 3 (the middle value). Mode = 3. Range = 13 − 2 = 11. The value 13 pulls the mean above the median.

items.q:
Heights of 6 basketball players (cm):
152, 168, 147, 175, 160, 149
What is the range?
items.e: Highest 175 cm, lowest 147 cm. Range = 175 − 147 = 28 cm. (152 − 149 = 3 uses the first and last values, and 175 − 149 = 26 misses the lowest, 147.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
What is the mean for the Lightning?
items.e: Add: 4 + 6 + 5 + 7 + 5 + 3 = 30. Divide by 6 games: 30 ÷ 6 = 5 goals. (30 is the total, 6 divides by 5, and 4 is the range.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
What is the median for the Storm?
items.e: In order: 1, 2, 2, 8, 8, 9. The two middle values are 2 and 8: (2 + 8) ÷ 2 = 5. (4.5 uses 1 and 8 from the unordered list, and 10 forgets to divide by 2.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
What is the mode for the Storm?
items.e: 2 appears twice and 8 appears twice, so the Storm has two modes: 2 and 8. (9 is the highest value.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
What is the range for each team?
items.e: Lightning: 7 − 3 = 4. Storm: 9 − 1 = 8. (7 and 9 are only the highest values, and 5 is the mean.)

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
Which team’s scores are more consistent?
items.e: Consistent means the values are close together. The Lightning’s range is 4 and the Storm’s is 8, so the Lightning’s scores are closer together.

items.q:
Goals scored by two ringette teams in 6 games:
Lightning: 4, 6, 5, 7, 5, 3
Storm: 9, 2, 1, 8, 8, 2
Which conclusion is supported by the data?
c: Both teams average 5 goals a game
The Storm is better: it scored 9
items.e: Both teams scored 30 goals in 6 games, so both means are 5. One high game (9) does not make the Storm better, and the Storm scored 1 goal in one game.

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by students in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
What is the median for 6B?
items.e: In order: 11, 12, 14, 15, 19, 20, 21. The middle (4th) value is 15. (21 is the middle of the unordered list, 16 is the mean, and 10 is the range.)

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by students in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
What is the mean for 6A?
items.e: Add: 14 + 16 + 15 + 17 + 16 + 18 + 16 = 112. Divide by 7: 112 ÷ 7 = 16 laps. (14 divides by 8, and 18 is the highest value.)

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by students in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
What is the range for 6B?
items.e: Highest 21, lowest 11. Range = 21 − 11 = 10. (14 − 12 = 2 uses the last and first values, and 4 is the range for 6A.)

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by students in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
Which sentence compares the two classes correctly?
c: Same mean, but 6B is more spread out
Same mean, but 6A is more spread out
items.e: Both means are 112 ÷ 7 = 16. The ranges are 4 (6A) and 10 (6B), so 6B is more spread out. The medians are 16 (6A) and 15 (6B).

items.q:
Laps skated in 10 minutes by students in two gym classes:
6A: 14, 16, 15, 17, 16, 18, 16
6B: 12, 20, 15, 21, 11, 19, 14
Which class has the higher median, and by how much?
items.e: 6A in order: 14, 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, 18, so its median is 16. 6B’s median is 15. 16 − 15 = 1 lap. (6 laps compares the ranges, 10 − 4.)

items.q: In which week were the two plants the same height?
items.e: The two lines start at the same point: both plants were 4 cm in week 1. After that, Plant A is always taller.

items.q: How much taller was Plant A than Plant B in week 5?
items.e: Week 5: Plant A is 26 cm and Plant B is 16 cm. 26 − 16 = 10 cm. (8 cm is the gap in week 4.)

items.q: Which plant grew faster?
c: Plant B: it grew more each week
Plant A: its line is steeper
Plant B: its line is lower
items.e: A steeper line means faster growth. Plant A grew 26 − 4 = 22 cm, and Plant B grew only 16 − 4 = 12 cm.

items.q: What is the mean growth of Plant A per week, from week 1 to week 5?
items.e: Plant A grew 26 − 4 = 22 cm. From week 1 to week 5 is 4 weeks: 22 ÷ 4 = 5.5 cm per week. (4.4 divides by 5, but there are only 4 weeks of growth. 6.5 forgets the 4 cm it started with.)

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 20:
Kai: 18, 17, 19, 18, 3
Amira: 16, 16, 15, 17, 16
Who has the higher mean?
items.e: Kai: 75 ÷ 5 = 15. Amira: 80 ÷ 5 = 16. Amira’s mean is higher. (18 is Kai’s median and mode.)

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 20:
Kai: 18, 17, 19, 18, 3
Amira: 16, 16, 15, 17, 16
Who has the higher median?
items.e: Kai in order: 3, 17, 18, 18, 19, so his median is 18. Amira in order: 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, so hers is 16.

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 20:
Kai: 18, 17, 19, 18, 3
Amira: 16, 16, 15, 17, 16
Kai was sick on the day he scored 3. Which measure best shows how he usually does?
c: The mean: it uses every score
items.e: 3 is far from Kai’s other scores (17 to 19). It pulls his mean down to 15. The median, 18, is not affected much by one outlier.

items.q:
Quiz scores out of 20:
Kai: 18, 17, 19, 18, 3
Amira: 16, 16, 15, 17, 16
Whose scores are more consistent?
items.e: Amira’s range is 17 − 15 = 2 and Kai’s is 19 − 3 = 16. A smaller range means the scores are closer together.

items.q: For the food drive, 6A (24 students) collected 120 cans. 6B (18 students) collected 108 cans. Which class collected more cans per student?
items.e: Use the mean, because the classes are different sizes. 6A: 120 ÷ 24 = 5. 6B: 108 ÷ 18 = 6. 6B collected more per student, even though its total is smaller.

items.q: How many students voted for the science centre?
items.e: The bar reaches the line for 46. (6 is the height above the bottom of the scale, which starts at 40, not 0.)

items.q: How many more votes did the science centre get than the zoo?
items.e: 46 − 42 = 4 votes. (6 reads only the part of the bar above 40, and 2 is the zoo bar above 40.)

items.q: The science centre bar looks 3 times as tall. Did it get 3 times as many votes?
c: Yes: its bar is 3 times as tall
No: the zoo got more votes
items.e: 3 × 42 = 126, but the science centre got only 46 votes. The bars start at 40, so we see only 6 and 2 of the votes: that makes one look 3 times the other.

items.q: Why does this graph make the difference look big?
c: The bars are the same colour
items.e: When the scale starts at 40, the bottom part of every bar is cut off. The small difference (4 votes) then looks huge.

items.q: To draw a fair bar graph of this data, where should the scale start?
items.e: Bar heights are fair to compare only when the scale starts at 0. Then the bars would be 46 and 42 high, and look almost the same.

items.q: How much more money was raised in 2026 than in 2022?
items.e: 2026: $1560. 2022: $1440. $1560 − $1440 = $120. ($160 measures from $1400, where the scale starts, and $40 is only the last year.)

items.q: A poster says, “Our school more than doubled the money it raised!” Is this supported?
items.e: Doubling $1440 gives $2880. The school raised $1560, an increase of only $120. The scale starts at $1400, so the line looks steeper than it is.

items.q: A bar graph’s scale is labelled 0, 5, 10, 50, 100, with equal spaces between the labels. Why is it misleading?
c: The equal spaces show unequal amounts
items.e: The space from 0 to 5 is the same as the space from 10 to 50, but one is 5 and the other is 40. Bars on this scale cannot be compared fairly.

items.q: A broken-line graph shows a town’s population in 2010, 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2026, with equal spaces between the years. Why is it misleading?
c: The years are not equally far apart
items.e: From 2010 to 2020 is 10 years, but the other gaps are 2 years. Equal spaces make 10 years of change look like 2 years.

items.q: A website says, “Kids love broccoli! 3 out of 4 kids we asked said yes.” They asked only 4 kids. Why is this claim weak?
c: The sample is far too small
3 out of 4 is less than half
items.e: 4 kids is a tiny sample. A different 4 kids could give a very different answer. (3 out of 4 is more than half.)

items.q: A survey at a hockey arena found that 45 of the 50 people asked said hockey is their favourite sport. A headline says, “90% of Canadians love hockey most!” What is the main problem?
c: People at an arena likely like hockey
items.e: The sample is biased: people at a hockey arena are more likely to choose hockey. 45 out of 50 is 90%, but only for those 50 people.

items.q: Weekly allowances of 6 friends: $10, $10, $12, $15, $8, $95. Owen says, “The typical allowance in our group is $25.” Which is a better typical value?
items.e: The mean is $150 ÷ 6 = $25, but 5 of the 6 friends get $15 or less. The $95 pulls the mean up. In order: 8, 10, 10, 12, 15, 95, so the median is (10 + 12) ÷ 2 = $11.

items.q: In a class of 28, pepperoni pizza got 9 votes, more than any other kind. Liam says, “Most of the class likes pepperoni best.” Is this supported?
c: No: pepperoni is not the mode
No: 9 of 28 is less than half
items.e: Pepperoni is the mode, but “most” means more than half. Half of 28 is 14, and only 9 students chose pepperoni.

items.q: At School A, 60 of the 600 students walk to school. At School B, 45 of the 150 students walk. At which school does a greater part of the students walk?
items.e: Compare parts of each school, not totals. A: 60 ÷ 600 = 10%. B: 45 ÷ 150 = 30%. School B has fewer walkers, but a greater part of its students walk.

items.q: A newsletter says, “Most of our students ran 1 km in under 6 minutes.” Is this supported?
c: Yes: the first bar is at 4
items.e: Under 6 minutes means the first two bars: 2 + 6 = 8 students. That is 8 of 30, less than half.

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by this graph?
items.e: Every point is below the 0 line, so the temperature stayed below 0 °C. It rose until 2 p.m., then fell. At 8 a.m. it was −18 °C, the coldest.

items.q: The mean number of goals for a hockey player is 2.5 a game. Hana says, “So in one game, the player scored 2.5 goals.” What is wrong?
c: The mean must be a whole number
The mean is the most common score
A mean does not have to be a data value
items.e: Goals are discrete: a player scores 2 or 3, never 2.5. The mean shares the total equally, so it can be a value that never happened. For example, 2 and 3 goals have a mean of 2.5.

items.q: A cereal box says, “Kids’ favourite! Chosen by 4 out of 5 kids.” Which question best checks this claim?
c: How many kids were asked, and who?
items.e: A claim like this depends on the sample. If only 5 kids were asked, or they were chosen by the cereal maker, the claim is weak.

items.q: An ad shows sales doubling with two maple leaf pictures. The second leaf is twice as wide and twice as tall. Why is this misleading?
c: It should be 3 times as tall
The big leaf looks 4 times as big
items.e: Doubling both the width and the height makes the area 2 × 2 = 4 times as big. The eye sees the area, so sales look 4 times bigger instead of 2 times.

items.q: The school play sold tickets on 4 nights: 85, 120, 96, 139. What is the mean number of tickets per night?
items.e: Add: 85 + 120 + 96 + 139 = 440. Divide by 4 nights: 440 ÷ 4 = 110 tickets. (88 divides by 5, and 54 is the range.)
